Fundamental — what it's worth: A weighted what-if off the published fair value — not a re-run DCF, and it never touches the Monte Carlo section below. The sizes come from the study’s own sensitivity grids, each of which re-runs the whole segment build, scaled down for the fact that only the cash-flow lenses move. Note which lever dominates: the cost of capital, not the operations. Three points of easing is worth more than a fifteen-percent swing in segment margins, because 85% of the enterprise value sits in the terminal year and the Egyptian discount rate is what compresses it. That is the study’s central claim in one control.
Technical & price structure: In plain terms: the business is excellent and the disagreement is about the price of Egyptian money. Discounted at a 26.6% pound cost of capital the shares are worth about EGP 70 against a 105 price; discount the hard-currency half of the cash flows at a dollar rate and the same model prints 86. What 105.20 buys is the market applying something even more generous than the dollar view — a bet that convertibility never binds and Egyptian easing arrives on schedule. That’s the gap.
Monte Carlo — where could the price go?: Our fundamental range tops out at EGP 0.95 even in the bull case — so unlike most names we cover, the whole simulated price cone sits ABOVE the fair-value range, not around it. Read that gap for what it is: the simulation prices where the tape can travel over three months, the study prices what the business is worth. A sustained move above EGP 0.95 on the fundamentals — collection landing, margins recovering, rates falling — is the point where we’d rebuild the study.

One Monte Carlo model, 50,000 paths, driven by the outside forces relevant to a hard-currency industrial exporter listed in a soft-currency market: the LME copper price, the EGP/USD path, the CBE policy corridor and the pace of easing, Egyptian inflation, Gulf and North African grid and infrastructure spending, the order book and its conversion rate, interconnector and data-centre demand for cable and transformers, energy and freight costs, convertibility and repatriation risk on the foreign earnings, and the free float — 11.6% of the shares, with 68% held by the family and 20% by Electra, which is what makes the tape thin.
